To summarize, the key findings of our research, stated in one sentence that includes all relevant information, are that

1) the incidence of vancomycin resistance enterococci in food samples was 10.7%, while in environmental samples 14.5%; 2) the vancomycin resistant enterococcal strains from meat and from the environment showed different plasmid profiles; 3) the glycopeptide resistance determinants were located on extrachromosomal elements in the VanA strains.
the prevalence of VRE was 26.5% in environmental samples and 35% in meat samples.
the presence of VRE in food is a serious concern and that the presence of glycopeptide resistance genes in food and environmental samples is a potential risk for human health.

the spread of VRE strains, and the location of the vanA determinant in VanA isolations.
the dissemination of vanA gene cluster in food and environment and its possible role in the spread of glycopeptide-resistant enterococcal infections in human.
the spread of glycopeptide resistance among meat and environmental isolates and the location of resistance determinants in Van A isolates.

the spread of VRE and VanA genes among meat and environment is a potential risk for human health.

VRE are not only a nosocomial problem but that food, and environment in general, may be a potential source for the dissemination of resistance genes.

VRE are not uncommon in meat and environment and the glycopeptide resistance determinants are not confined to enterococci but may be present in other bacteria as well.
